entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 12 Ho 12:1-14 . Reproof of Ephraim and Judah: Their Father Jacob Ought to Be a Pattern to Them. This prophecy was delivered about the time of Israel's seeking the aid of the Egyptian king So, in violation of their covenant with Assyria (see Ho 12:1 ). He exhorts them to follow their father Jacob's persevering prayerfulness, which brought God's favor upon him. As God is unchangeable, He will show the same favor to Jacob's posterity as He did to Jacob, if, like him, they seek God. 1. feedeth on wind-- ( Pr 15:14 ; Is 44:20 ). Followeth after vain objects, such as alliances with idolaters and their idols (compare Ho 8:7 ). east wind-- the simoon, blowing from the desert east of Palestine, which not only does not benefit, but does injury. Israel follows not only things vain, but things pernicious (compare Job 15:2 ). increaseth lies-- accumulates lie upon lie, that is, impostures wherewith they deceive themselves, forsaking the truth of God. desolation-- violent oppressions practised by Israel [Maurer]. Acts which would prove the cause of Israel's own desolation [Calvin]. covenant with ... Assyrians-- ( Ho 5:13 ; 7:11 ). oil ... into Egypt-- as a present from Israel to secure Egypt's alliance ( Is 30:6 ; 57:9 ; compare 2Ki 17:4 ). Palestine was famed for oil ( Eze 27:17 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12398"/><div sID="gen22722" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12398"/><hi type="bold">3. He--</hi>Jacob, contrasted with his degenerate descendants, called by his name, Jacob (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.2">Ho 12:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">Mi 2:7</reference>). He took Esau by the heel in the womb in order to obtain, if possible, the privileges of the first-born (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.22-Gen.25.26">Ge 25:22-26</reference>), whence he took his name, Jacob, meaning "supplanter"; and again, by his strength, prevailed in wrestling with God for a blessing (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.24-Gen.32.29">Ge 32:24-29</reference>); whereas ye disregard My promises, putting your confidence in idols and foreign alliances. He conquered God, ye are the slaves of idols. Only have Jehovah on your side, and ye are stronger than Edom, or even Assyria. So the spiritual Israel lays hold of the heel of Jesus, "the First-born of many brethren," being born again of the Holy Spirit. Having no right in themselves to the inheritance, they lay hold of the bruised heel, the humanity of Christ crucified, and let not go their hold of Him who is not, as Esau, a curse (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">He 12:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.17">17</reference>), but, by becoming a curse for us, is a blessing to us.<div eID="gen22722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">power with God--</hi>referring to his name, "Israel," prince of God, acquired on that occasion (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.11.12">Mt 11:12</reference>). As the promised Canaan had to be gained forcibly by Israel, so heaven by the faithful (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.13.24">Lu 13:24</reference>). "Strive," literally, "as in the agony of a contest." So the Canaanitess (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.22">Mt 15:22</reference>).<div eID="gen22723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his strength--</hi>which lay in his conscious weakness, whence, when his thigh was put out of joint by God, he hung upon Him. To seek strength was his object; to grant it, God's. Yet God's mode of procedure was strange. In human form He tries as it were to throw Jacob down. When simple wrestling was not enough, He does what seems to ensure Jacob's fall, dislocating his thigh joint, so that he could no longer stand. Yet it was then that Jacob prevailed. Thus God teaches us the irresistible might of conscious weakness. For when weak in ourselves, we are strong by His strength put in us (<reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.5">Is 27:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">2Co 12:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen22724" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12399"/><div sID="gen22725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12399"/><hi type="bold">4. the angel--</hi>the uncreated Angel of the Covenant, as God the Son appears in the Old Testament (Mal 3:1).<div eID="gen22725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made supplication--</hi><reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Ge 32:26</reference>: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."<div eID="gen22726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he found him--</hi>The angel found Jacob, when he was fleeing from Esau into Syria: the Lord appearing to him "in Beth-el" (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.11-Gen.19.35">Ge 28:11-19; 35</reference>:1). What God there spoke to Jacob appertains to us. God's promises to him belong to all his posterity who follow in the steps of his prayerful faith. <div eID="gen22728" type="x-p"/>

Lord God--</hi>Jehovah, a name implying His immutable constancy to His promises. From the Hebrew root, meaning "existence." "He that is, was, and is to be," always the same (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.8">He 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.4">Re 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Exod.3.14">Ex 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">6:3</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12402"/><div sID="gen22736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12402"/><hi type="bold">7. merchant--</hi>a play on the double sense of the Hebrew, "Canaan," that is, a Canaanite and a "merchant" <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.3">Eze 16:3</reference>: "Thy birth is ... of Canaan." They who naturally were descendants of pious Jacob had become virtually Canaanites, who were proverbial as cheating merchants (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.11">Is 23:11</reference>, Margin), the greatest reproach to Israel, who despised Canaan. The Phoenicians called themselves Canaanites or merchants (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.8">Is 23:8</reference>).<div eID="gen22736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oppress--</hi>open violence: as the "balances of deceit" imply fraud. <div eID="gen22737" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12404"/><div sID="gen22743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12404"/><hi type="bold">9. And--</hi>rather, "And yet." Though Israel deserves to be cast off for ever, yet I am still what I have been from the time of My delivering them out of Egypt, their covenant God; therefore, "I will yet make thee to dwell in tabernacles," that is, to keep the feast of tabernacles again in remembrance of a new deliverance out of bondage. Fulfilled primarily at the return from Babylon (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.17">Ne 8:17</reference>). Fully and antitypically to be fulfilled at the final restoration from the present dispersion (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Lev.23.42">Le 23:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.43">43</reference>). <div eID="gen22743" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9. And-- rather, "And yet." Though Israel deserves to be cast off for ever, yet I am still what I have been from the time of My delivering them out of Egypt, their covenant God; therefore, "I will yet make thee to dwell in tabernacles," that is, to keep the feast of tabernacles again in remembrance of a new deliverance out of bondage. Fulfilled primarily at the return from Babylon ( Ne 8:17 ). Fully and antitypically to be fulfilled at the final restoration from the present dispersion ( Zec 14:16 ; compare Le 23:42 , 43 ).

Is there iniquity in Gilead?--</hi>He asks the question, not as if the answer was doubtful, but to strengthen the affirmation: "Surely they are vanity"; or as Maurer translates, "They are nothing but iniquity." Iniquity, especially idolatry, in Scripture is often termed "vanity." <reference osisRef="Prov.13.11">Pr 13:11</reference>: "Wealth gotten by vanity," that is, iniquity. <reference osisRef="Isa.41.29">Is 41:29</reference>: "They are all vanity ... images." "Gilead" refers to Mizpah-gilead, a city representing the region beyond Jordan (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.8">Ho 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.11.29">Jud 11:29</reference>); as "Gilgal," the region on this side of Jordan (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Ho 4:15</reference>). In all quarters alike they are utterly vile.<div eID="gen22746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their altars are as heaps in the furrows--</hi>that is, as numerous as such heaps: namely, the heaps of stones cleared out of a stony field. An appropriate image, as at a distance they look like altars (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">Ho 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">8:11</reference>). As the third member in the parallelism answers to the first, "Gilgal" to "Gilead," so the fourth to the second, "altars" to "vanity." The word "heaps" alludes to the name "Gilgal," meaning "a heap of stones." The very scene of the general circumcision of the people, and of the solemn passover kept after crossing Jordan, is now the stronghold of Israel's idolatry. <div eID="gen22747" type="x-p"/>

Jacob fled ... served--</hi>Though ye pride yourselves on the great name of "Israel," forget not that your progenitor was the same Jacob who was a fugitive, and who served for Rachel fourteen years. He forgot not ME who delivered him when fleeing from Esau, and when oppressed by Laban (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.5">Ge 28:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.29.20">29:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">De 26:5</reference>). Ye, though delivered from Egypt (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.13">Ho 12:13</reference>), and loaded with My favors, are yet unwilling to return to Me.<div eID="gen22748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">country of Syria--</hi>the champaign region of Syria, the portion lying between the Tigris and Euphrates, hence called Mesopotamia. Padan-aram means the same, that is, "Low Syria," as opposed to Aramea (meaning the "high country") or Syria (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.7">Ge 48:7</reference>). <div eID="gen22749" type="x-p"/>
